title: The Clutter Above Us

lines.text: Good morning. Let's talk about something that rarely makes the news: the clutter in orbit around the Earth.
Since the first satellite was launched, thousands of objects have been left up there, including dead satellites, spent rocket stages and fragments from collisions.

Because these objects travel at several kilometres every second, even a tiny fragment carries enormous energy. Space shuttle windows were sometimes damaged by flecks of paint, which tells you something.
So the real danger isn't the large pieces, which can be tracked, but the countless small ones that can't.
In the late nineteen-seventies, a scientist called Donald Kessler proposed that, beyond a certain density, collisions would create debris that would cause further collisions, in a chain reaction.
This is now known as the Kessler syndrome. It doesn't mean that space would suddenly become impassable, but that certain orbits could become progressively harder to use.
Now, who is responsible? Agencies have typically had their satellites designed to leave orbit at the end of their lives, but compliance has been uneven.
Operators who fail to do so don't generally have their licences withdrawn, because there's no effective enforcement. That's the weak link.
Some companies now offer to have dead satellites removed, using robotic arms or nets. The technology is real, though it's still at an early stage and far from cheap.
An insurer, for example, might one day insist that every satellite be built with a removal mechanism. If that happens, I'd expect behaviour to change quickly.
I'd add that the problem is not purely technical. It's a question of who pays when the debris belongs to a company that has gone bankrupt.
International law tends to say that an owner remains responsible for an object in space. In practice, that has rarely been tested.
So we're facing a classic shared-resource problem. Everyone benefits from orbit, and nobody wants to be the one to clean it up.
For next week, I'd like you to find a recent proposal for debris removal and be prepared to say who should foot the bill.

title: The Nurse Who Walked Away
focus: Verb patterns (resent, regret, can't help, risk, be committed to)

lines.text: Joel, you left nursing after eleven years. Do you resent having had to make that choice?
Resent might be too strong. I regret not leaving earlier, though, and I can't help wondering whether I'd have been a better nurse if I'd taken a break.
What wore you down in the end?

Not the patients. People assume it's the emotional side, but I'd never avoid a difficult conversation. It was the constant understaffing, which meant skipping breaks, staying late, and feeling that I was always letting someone down.
That sounds exhausting.
It was. I'd stopped noticing it, which is the dangerous part. Burnout rarely announces itself. You just find that you've stopped caring about things you used to love.
Did anyone intervene?
My manager suggested taking a holiday, which was kind, but it was like recommending a plaster for a broken leg.
Is that fair? She was trying to help.
She was, and I don't want to criticise her. She was working under the same pressure. But a holiday doesn't change the rota.
So what would help?
Hiring enough staff, obviously, but also being allowed to refuse extra shifts without being made to feel guilty. Hospitals risk losing their best people by relying on goodwill.
Do you miss it?
Every day, which surprises me. I'm committed to caring for people, just not in that system, so now I teach first aid.
That sounds like a happy ending.
A cautious one. I'd recommend anyone in that position to consider leaving before they're forced to.
Thank you for your honesty.

title: Who Owns a Style?
focus: Result and manner clauses (so… that, such… that, as if, as though)

lines.text: Tonight: should artists be paid when their work is used to train image generators? Ms Duarte, you're an illustrator.
I am, and I feel strongly about this. My style took twenty years to develop, and it was used by a system in such a way that anyone can now reproduce it in seconds.
I understand the frustration, but the law has to be careful. Style isn't generally protected. If it were, so much creative work would be restricted that artists themselves would suffer.
That's too convenient. The system doesn't merely learn from my work as a student might. It was fed so many images that it can imitate me as if I'd drawn the result myself.
Imitation isn't copying, though. Human artists have always learned by imitating. The question is whether a machine's learning should be treated the same way.
Mr Kim, is that your view?
It's the strongest argument on the other side, honestly. The scale is so different that the old comparison may not hold.
Thank you. A person can only imitate so many people in a lifetime. The machine does it for millions of artists at once, and so quickly that no one can compete.
That concession matters. I'd accept that a licensing scheme might be fair, such that artists could opt in and be paid.
Opt in, not opt out. If I have to find every company that has used my work, it's as though the burden has been put on the victim.
That's persuasive, although it would be complicated to run. So many works have no clear owner that registering them would be a huge task.
Is there a practical middle path?
Collective licensing, perhaps, in which a fund pays artists based on how often their work is used.
Something like that exists for music, and it works well enough that nobody seriously proposes abolishing it.
A fair note to end on. Thank you both.

title: Fewer Fish, Fewer Boats?
focus: Paraphrasing and checking understanding (if I understand you correctly, so what you're saying is)

lines.text: Captain Souza, thank you for coming. As you know, scientists have recommended a lower catch for next season.
I've read the report. If I understand it correctly, they're saying the stock has fallen, but they also admit they're not certain by how much.
That's fair. They describe the margin of error as considerable, which is why they've recommended caution.
So what you're saying is that you're cutting our quota on the basis of an estimate.
I'd put it differently. The estimate is the best we have, and if it's wrong in either direction, we'd rather it erred on the side of the fish.
Easy to say if you're not the one paying the loan on the boat. My crew has already been told to expect a normal season.
I appreciate that. Let me check I've understood your position: you can accept a cut, but not a sudden one.
Exactly. A gradual reduction over three seasons, with a review each year, would be something I could take to the others.
Review based on what?
On survey data collected jointly, so that we're not just taking your word for it, nor you ours.
That's constructive. I'd want the data to be collected by an independent party, though, so that nobody can question it.
Agreed, as long as fishers have a seat on the oversight group.
I think that's possible. May I summarise? A phased cut over three seasons, annual joint reviews, independent data, and fishers represented on the oversight group.
That's it, though I'd add compensation for the boats that can't operate in the first year.
I can't commit to that today, but I'll take it to the ministry and let you know by the end of the month.

title: Walking Through a Memory
focus: Relative clauses with prepositions (in which, with which, by which, for whom)

lines.text: Good afternoon. I'd like to talk about a technique that is thousands of years old, and one that cognitive scientists have taken seriously: the memory palace.
The method, which was described by ancient Greek and Roman writers on oratory, works by placing the things you want to remember in an imagined building.
Imagine a house with which you're thoroughly familiar. You walk through the front door and, in the hallway, you place the first item on your list, vividly, in a way that's slightly absurd.
Then you move to the kitchen and place the second. To recall the list, you simply walk through the house again.
Why does it work? The explanation to which most researchers subscribe is that human memory is far better at remembering places and images than abstract lists.
Our ancestors, for whom finding food depended on remembering where it was, were presumably selected for exactly that ability.
The technique has been used by competitors in memory championships, many of whom can memorise a shuffled pack of cards in remarkably short times.
What's interesting is that studies of such competitors suggest that they aren't born with exceptional memories. The training by which they improve is largely about method.
That's encouraging for the rest of us, but I should add a caveat. The method is excellent for lists and sequences, whereas it's far less useful for understanding.
Memorising the order of the planets is one thing. Grasping the reason why a planet follows its orbit is quite another.
There's also a question about the kind of person for whom this would be worth the effort. If you rarely need to recall long lists, the time spent building palaces may not pay off.
But for students who must learn long sequences, such as anatomy or legal articles, there's some evidence that it helps, particularly when time is short.
My own experience, in which I used the technique before an exam, was that it worked, though I felt rather silly placing a skeleton in my bathroom.
For the practical session, please prepare a palace, ideally a place that you know well, and a list of twenty items, which I'll give you tomorrow.

options: Students who must learn long sequences
questions.explain_es: 'For students who must learn long sequences, such as anatomy or legal articles, there's some evidence that it helps.'

title: Joining Her in Her World

lines.text: Hugo, it's good to see you. How is your mother?
Some days she's herself, and some days she isn't. Yesterday she asked me when my father was coming home, and he died years ago.
That must be hard. What did you say?
I used to correct her, you know. Then I realised that I was making her grieve all over again. Wouldn't you do the same?
I think I might. It's about kindness, isn't it, rather than strict accuracy?
That's how I've come to see it. The nurse told me to join her in her world, not drag her into mine.
Wise advice. Does it get easier?
In some ways. But how does one prepare for gradually losing someone who's still sitting in the room?
I don't think one can, really. You're grieving while still caring, which is a strange position, isn't it?
It is. And people mean well, but they say things like, at least she's comfortable, as though that settles it.
As though it were that simple.
Right. Which is why it helps to talk to someone who has been through it. You've been through it, haven't you?
With my aunt, yes. And what I learned is that you have to look after yourself too, otherwise you can't look after anyone.
My sister keeps telling me the same. You'd think I'd have listened by now, wouldn't you?
It's hard to hear when you're exhausted. Would an afternoon off help?
It would, actually. Thank you for asking.

title: Who Gets Asked Before the Shutter Clicks?
focus: Passive voice with modals (ought to have been asked, may be exploited, can be blurred)

lines.text: Let's turn to consent. A well-known photograph from the nineteen-thirties shows a migrant worker with her children, and it became a symbol of an era. The woman in it later said she had gained nothing from it. Omar, what's your reaction?
Honestly, I think she ought to have been asked, and perhaps compensated. A picture like that can't be separated from the fame it generated.
I'm not sure that's fair. Times have changed, and the photographer can't be judged by today's standards. The image might never have been seen if she had stopped to negotiate.
That's a convenient argument. Nobody would say it should be excused in a similar case today.
Eleni, is it about the past or the present?
Both, in a way. Today a photographer must be seen to act responsibly, and the people in the pictures should be shown the result if they want.
Shown, or asked beforehand?
Asked, ideally. But in a crisis, such as a disaster, consent can't always be obtained, and the images may be needed as evidence.
Then the images could be used while the subjects are protected, couldn't they? Faces can be blurred.
That depends. A blurred face can't be recognised, but it also can't move us. Some of the power is lost.
That's the central tension. Images must be truthful, and yet they ought not to be exploited.
And who decides what counts as exploitation?
Increasingly, the subjects themselves, which is a welcome development. Several agencies now require that the people photographed should be informed how images will be used.
That seems sensible. It doesn't solve everything, but it can't hurt.
For next week, I'd like each of you to write a short code of practice that could be applied by a news agency. Be ready to defend it.

title: Taxing Wealth, Not Just Income
focus: Concession and rebuttal (admittedly, granted, to be fair, even so)

lines.text: Tonight we're discussing a wealth tax. Doctor Okoye, you're in favour. Why?
Because wealth has become concentrated in a way that income tax doesn't reach. Admittedly, the idea isn't new, but the scale of the gap is.
Granted, the gap is real. But a tax on assets, as opposed to income, is hard to administer. How do you value a family business that isn't for sale?
That's a fair difficulty. Even so, tax authorities value property every year, and they manage it, more or less.
More or less is the problem. Valuations can be disputed for years, and the cost to the authorities may exceed what they collect.
Doctor Okoye?
It's possible, I'll concede, though evidence on that is mixed. Some countries tried it and gave up, whereas others have kept it. The details matter enormously.
To be fair, the details are exactly what I'm worried about. Wealthy people can move their assets, or themselves, abroad.
Admittedly, that's a risk. But a well-designed tax applies when someone leaves, so they can't escape it simply by moving.
That would be difficult to enforce. And there's the matter of fairness: a farmer with valuable land but little cash would be forced to sell.
I'd agree that's unjust. A sensible design would allow payment in instalments, and set the threshold high enough to spare the farmer.
Then we agree on something. Though in that case, the tax would raise much less than its supporters claim.
Possibly, though less isn't nothing, and it might carry a symbolic importance.
Symbols don't build hospitals.
That seems a fitting place to stop. Thank you both.

title: Slower Than You Think
focus: Comparative structures (far more, nowhere near as, by far the, not nearly as)

lines.text: You've coached runners for twenty years. What's the biggest mistake beginners make?
By far the commonest is doing too much too soon. They're nowhere near as fit as they think they are, and the enthusiasm outruns the body.
So how should a beginner start?
Far more slowly than feels natural. The first few weeks should feel almost embarrassingly easy. Tendons adapt much more slowly than muscles, which is why injuries appear in week six or seven.
Is speed training important?
Not nearly as important as people think. Most of the fitness comes from running slowly, and a little speed work on top is plenty.
That's counterintuitive.
It is, and it's the single hardest thing to convince runners of. We're a good deal more competitive than we admit.
What about the mental side?
Considerably more important than the physical side in the last stage of a marathon. The legs know what to do; it's the head that has to agree.
Can you train the mind?
To a degree. Practising how to cope when it's going badly is much more useful than imagining that it won't.
Any advice for race day?
Go out slower than you want to. The earlier you hurry, the more you pay later, and no one has ever regretted starting a little too gently.
Do you still run yourself?
Far less than I'd like, but I'm in a better position to enjoy it. I'm no longer trying to beat anyone.
